Routine oil at Paul's regular shop (Express Oil, Moreland Ave) on live coupons — and a FREE second-opinion look at the coolant leak while it's on the lift. GATE FIRST (call 404-659-6225): confirm they stock VW 502.00-approved oil (5W-40 preferred; a 502.00 5W-30 is also fine) + get the out-the-door price with $20-off — the coupon covers standard oil only and voids with customer-supplied oil, so gate on VW 502.00 (a 502.00 5W-30 is fine, 5W-40 preferred for the Stage-1 tune) — the real walk-away is a generic/dexos 5W-30 with NO 502.00 (then walk to Autobahn). If oil's a go: stack the FREE tire rotation (RTE026) + $15-off alignment (ASR026), and ask them to inspect + pressure-test the coolant leak (known EA888 failure = plastic water pump + thermostat housing). Coolant is VW G13 (pink) ONLY — if they don't stock it, inspect only, add nothing. Get any leak finding + repair estimate IN WRITING as a benchmark vs Autobahn. Coupons: $39.99 conv / $59.99 hi-mileage (YID726, thru 7/11) or $20-off (YDCD26, thru 7/31); free rotation + alignment thru 7/31. Full question list: .research/2026-07-08-gti-express-oil-coupons.md.

Done — running NGK R7437-8 racing plugs (the APR Stage-1 heat range), installed and doing well. These are one range colder than stock; the R7437-9 Eurofed used with the 2022 tune is the Stage-3 plug (over-cold here) and is now hard to find, so the -8 is the correct pick, not a compromise. NEXT CHANGE reminder: gap to 0.024" (they ship at 0.028" — close them down), torque ~25 Nm / 18 ft-lb dry (no anti-seize — NGK's plating already anti-seizes), dielectric grease in the coil boots, and change roughly every ~20k mi on the tune. Full spec + sources in .research/2026-07-14-gti-spark-plug-setup.md.

Get a second key before you ever need it — you still have one working key, so this is a cheap “add-a-key” job, not the all-keys-lost nightmare. Yours is the flip-key-with-KESSY (Comfort Access) type — SPEC CONFIRMED off Paul's own key (2026-07-14, read off the fob + web-verified): genuine Hella OEM, FCC ID NBGFS12P01, VW part 5G0 959 752 BE family (MK7 / MQB platform), 315 MHz US, MQB48 transponder, HU66 blade, CR2025 battery, 4-button. ⚠️ THIS CORRECTS AN EARLIER SPEC: the Facebook Marketplace pair read 5K0 837 202 AK / FCC NBG010206T — a DIFFERENT, older (non-MK7) generation. Do NOT buy those for this car; they're the wrong key and would be the classic won't-program money-pit. Source to NBGFS12P01 / 5G0 959 752. Two routes: a VW-capable MOBILE locksmith (comes to you, one visit, ~$250–400, roughly 40–60% under dealer) or a VW dealer (either Jim Ellis Chamblee — right by Autobahn, so you can do it the same trip as the GTI service — or Jim Ellis Kennesaw, which is on the way to the property; OEM but usually order-then-return = 2 trips, ~$350–450; bundle it with the free 16V647 recall check + a written 90k estimate). The catch with USED keys (e.g. a Facebook Marketplace pair): the MK7 is MQB, so registering a key needs dealer FAZIT online access or an MQB-capable locksmith, and a used fob still married to another car can REFUSE to program (people have burned $120+ trying). Before buying used, confirm it’s virgin/resettable AND line up someone who’ll program used MQB keys — otherwise a new aftermarket NBGFS12P01 / 5G0 959 752 fob (~$35–80) programs clean. Programming is the gated cost either way (~$60–150). On the dealer trip: skip any "free multi-point inspection" as a to-do list (dealer pricing + upsell, and you trust Autobahn for the real diagnosis) — but DO grab the dealer-only freebies: the free recall check + any recall work (16V647 EVAP etc.), and optionally a free written estimate to use as a price benchmark against Autobahn. While it's there for the freebies, it costs nothing to have them also eyeball the two open 'verify at next visit' items — the coolant level and the brake-pad thickness — just don't let those turn into an upsell list. — RECALL NOTE: a suction-jet-pump safety recall was already performed at Jim Ellis 3/2025 (@ ~73.6k); still worth running a fresh free recall check by VIN on the dealer trip in case anything new has been issued.

Paul does these himself (DIY) — not an Autobahn job. Engine air filter: VW OEM 5Q0 129 620 B. Cabin filter: VW OEM 5Q0 819 644 A (activated-carbon combination filter). Both are easy at-home swaps; pick them up and do them at the property.

Direct injection builds carbon on the intake valves; 80–100k is the window to inspect and walnut-blast — at ~81k you're just at the front edge, so it may well not be needed yet. Have the shop scope it and tell you how bad it is before you commit to the job.
No fixed interval; stretch usually needs action at 120–150k. A quick VCDS / OBDeleven read now gives a baseline — worth it on a tuned car.
Both are common softening/failure points on tuned MK7s. Cheap to inspect while it's at this visit.

You recall the brakes looking OK recently, and the records back that up — front brakes done 2022 (Eurofed/Autohaus), rears at Midas 2022. On 7/11/26 Express gave it an overall look-over and flagged nothing on the brakes — read: no red flags, likely fine. (Caveat: their checklist measures brake FLUID level, not pad thickness, so there's no actual pad number on record yet.) No action needed; just confirm pad thickness at the next shop visit — it rides along for free with the spare-key dealer trip or the Autobahn visit (see those items). Low priority.

The strikers (where the latches close) can be adjusted to reposition the tailgate, so there's room to dial it in — needs playing with. Older truck; not chasing perfection. PARTS (DIY, installed): rear-window lift motor = Dorman 742-251; tailgate striker bushing = Dorman 38424 (installed to address the tailgate-angle/alignment). Sourced from the Amazon parts record. The motor + wiring troubleshooting ran **Sept–Oct 2025** (the switch-short saga — new fuses + the under-dash circuit breaker restored operation); the glass has worked since. ✅ DONE — Paul confirmed still operating correctly 2026-07-13.

Refinish sequence — Phase 1: the gate before anything comes apart. Operating rule (Paul): assume WE handle it ourselves, work each spot DIY as far as our skill+tools reach, escalate only when genuinely beyond us. The full repaint is the enabler — no need to preserve/blend old paint, so grind-fill-sand-prime is just prep. Larry's prep+prime is the safety net for anything marginal. Known so far: small rust around the wheel wells + a few minor dents (plus the bed/tailgate spot — separate item). Full DIY ladder + the hand-off line + wheel-arch bubble learnings + bed-corner section all in guides/bolores-bodywork-rust-dents.md. KEY: a wheel-arch bubble is the tip, not the extent — rust spreads under good-looking paint, so scope off what you find once a bubble's ground back to metal, not off the surface. NEXT ACTION — full walk-around (guides/bolores-walkaround.md), log each spot with a Rung # (1 cleanup / 2 patch / 3 weld-or-hand-off). Gates the repaint.

Small but significant rust in the bed near the tailgate where water got in (Paul flagged 2026-06-22). Textbook full-size Bronco failure: the tailgate leaks (glass sweep + failed access-panel barrier) and rots the rear bed corners. TWO jobs, order matters: (1) fix the leak source first — tailgate weatherstrip, esp. the corner pieces, + redo the access-panel barrier — or new metal just rots again; (2) repair the metal: open it up to find the true extent, then Rung 1 (clean+convert+prime) if it's only scale, or Rung 2 (cut back + bonded 3M patch, or weld) if it's perforated. Bed floor isn't frame-structural, so a bonded-and-rustproofed patch is legit. Likely ours to handle. AWAITING Paul: photos + detail (size, gone-through?, how far the wet spread). Method in guides/bolores-bodywork-rust-dents.md.

Supersedes the old 'failing clear coat' plan — instead of correcting the clear coat, doing a full refinish. Larry cleans, preps and primes at his place; his buddy's shop sprays. Scope locked (2026-06-22): exterior + interior together — matching a fresh body to a tired interior would mean redoing it, so converging is better for value and means only one teardown. Colors: original factory two-tone — Cabernet Red (upper) over Light Chestnut (lower), per the paint block below; staying factory protects resale value. Interior panels sprayed a fresh, consistent chestnut — this also removes the hard 'match a faded panel' problem from the door-panel repair. Hand the shop the door cert-label codes, or confirm they spectro-scan off the truck. Gated on the bodywork scope (Phase 1). No deadline — paint lands after all the teardown-window work is done. Full sequence in guides/bolores-door-panel-repair.md.

Actuator already replaced with no fix, so the signal isn't reaching it. Next: meter power switch → actuator. Prime suspect is the door-jamb boot wiring (flexes and cracks inside the rubber boot where you can't see it); also check the switch and its ground. (Refinish sequence — Phase 2: the door teardown. Do it in one door-open session alongside the panel repair, the handle-mount check, and door sound-deadening.) TIMELINE: the driver-side actuator was replaced ~Jan 2026 (no fix), and a further attempt fitting a new motor to the actuator ran ~Feb 2026 — STILL no response, so it's not the actuator, it's upstream. Confirms the wiring diagnosis (door-jamb boot wiring the prime suspect). Paul has been deferring the wire-metering step; that's the next move (last hands-on ~Feb 2026).

Cruise is inoperative — no response from the steering-wheel buttons. The servo hardware and the dual-cable throttle linkage are both present, but the servo's vacuum hoses are disconnected/misrouted. Plan: reconnect the vacuum supply + vent lines and cap any open ports, inspect the old hoses for cracks, and test the servo diaphragm for vacuum hold (the common internal-leak failure) before reassembly. If it still won't engage after that, work the electrical side — the brake (BOO) switch, the speed signal (VSS), the steering-wheel switch pod, and the cruise amplifier/module behind the glove box, and confirm the 3-pin cruise connector is seated. A dig-in-when-you're-under-the-dash job; pairs naturally with the Phase-2 dash/steering-column work.

Cracked through with broken clip mounts. Plan is repair-in-place, not replace: back-reinforce the cracks with heat-formed ABS sheet, rebuild the broken clip pockets from ABS, then flexible-fill the show face (3M EZ Sand 35887 — verified the right product, sold on Amazon too) and SAND TO PRIMER-READY. No more self color-matching — the paint shop sprays the chestnut as part of the interior refinish, which kills the hardest part of this job. Full materials list + step-by-step at guides/bolores-door-panel-repair.md. Gate: confirm the panel's plastic type (ABS vs PP) before buying adhesives. Phase-2 door teardown — done together with the lock, the handle-mount check, and door deadening. Still gates the audio build — a loose panel rattles and ruins subs. Fallback if the repair doesn't hold: source an '87–91 Bronco/F-series chestnut panel (long lead). PARTS (DIY, installed): new door-trim panel retainer clips = Icyhaws (Ford F150/Bronco) — fitted to rebuild the broken clip pockets.

Check first: does either INSIDE door handle feel loose/floppy or fail to pull the latch? On '80–'97 OBS Fords the sheet metal behind the inside handle fatigues and cracks — the classic 'roll the window down to get out' failure. If present (likely on an '89), the proven fix is a 14-ga steel reinforcement plate that rivets onto the inner door metal — no welding, rivets included; strong forum track record (Solo Motorsports / OBS Solutions / Bronco Graveyard, also generic on eBay/Amazon). Sold as a driver+passenger pair, so do both doors while they're open in Phase 2. Adds zero extra teardown.

Small tear in the dash pad's vinyl/leather — Paul wants it repaired. Full step-by-step (clean → trim → sub-patch → thin-layer flexible compound → grain-set → color) in guides/bolores-dash-vinyl-repair.md. Color converges with the interior refinish: repair the substrate now, let the chestnut spray/dye pass color it with the rest. Grain-matching is the make-or-break for invisibility; use FLEXIBLE compound (the dash flexes + bakes) never rigid filler. OPEN QUESTION: is the dash pad going to the booth, getting dyed in place, or capped? Decide with the interior piece-list. (If the pad turns out cracked across a large area, the durable fix is a dash cap, not many small repairs.)

Front driver seat needs an upholstery repair — find a local auto-upholstery / trim shop and get a quote. Match the chestnut interior. Runs in parallel at the trim shop during the paint window; reinstall during reassembly.

Replacement headliner — installs during reassembly (Phase 4), right after the roof sound-deadening goes in: the headliner is down anyway for the deadener, so they're one job. Can also pair with the upholstery shop visit.

Sound-deadening (doors, floor, roof). The key realization (2026-06-22): this is NOT a separate project — it's the first step of reassembly after paint, and nearly free in teardown terms because every surface it needs is already exposed by work you're already doing: door shells (panels off), floor pans (carpet up, seats out at the trim shop), roof (headliner down). Goes on after the body's painted, before panels/carpet/headliner go back. Refinish sequence — Phase 4.

The everyday listening system is in and playing — installed together ~Feb 2026. Fitted a RetroSound (Liberty-type) head unit, then did all four speakers in the same go: FRONT doors = Infinity Kappa 63XF 6.5" (165 mm) two-way coaxials (open-box from Creative Audio, Feb 2026, order #1000140355) on their NVX silicone baffles; REAR = Infinity Kappa 86CFX 6×8 coaxials (a separate purchase). The truck's old external amp didn't work, so it was pulled — all four speakers now run straight off the head unit. Sounds good as-is; the amp + subwoofer build below is a down-the-road upgrade, not a fix.

The audio upgrade beyond the head-unit-only setup — an amp + subwoofers, deliberately last (Phase 5), after the door panels are solid (repaired + reinforced) and the sound-deadening's done so it sings. One move that saves a whole future teardown: PRE-RUN the amp/sub wiring during the Phase-2 door + interior teardown, even though the gear goes in last. Amp + subs not yet purchased (confirmed 2026-07-14).

The plastic screw bosses that hold the rear-window up/down and rear-defrost switches into the trim (lower-left of the steering column) had cracked through over time, leaving the switches loose. Rebuilt the bosses using heat-shrink tubing as a sleeve/form and JB Weld to recreate threadable mounting posts. Switches now mount solidly — arguably more durable than the original brittle plastic. See technique: "Screw-boss rebuild."

The instrument-cluster backlight had a burned-out gauge light — replaced it with a purpose-bought replacement bulb sourced for the job (~late 2025). A separate fix from the dome/map/dash warm-LED re-bulb below (different bulb, different sitting).

restoration.item: Electrical fault — total power loss when steering
restoration.detail:
RESOLVED 2026-07-03 — Paul got the power-loss fault worked out; the bike powers up cleanly again with a constant, steady flow. THE ACTUAL FIX (not the planned conductor splice): worked the connectors up by the steering head — reseated the individual wires/pins in their plastic connector housings, cleaned the contacts with electrical contact cleaner, then pressed the connectors firmly back together; that alone restored a constant flow. Also patched a couple of questionable wire joints and wrapped everything in electrical tape for a more durable seal. So the root cause was really dirty/loose connector contacts at the flex point, not a cleanly-broken conductor. WATCH FOR RECURRENCE: the tape seal is less permanent than adhesive-lined heat-shrink, and if the fault ever returns when turning the bars, the fallback is to cut the suspect section back to bright copper and solder-splice it with adhesive heat-shrink (the originally-planned repair).

— Original diagnosis, kept for reference —
DIAGNOSED 2026-06-13 — traced end to end with a multimeter. The fault is a broken/fatigued conductor in the steering-head harness (the bundle that flexes when you turn the bars), confirmed by wiggle-testing the wires and watching the headlight cut on and off. THE TRAIL: (1) Battery good — 12.7V at the posts, both cables tight. (2) Main fuse good — there are two 20A blade fuses in the holder above the battery; the live one reads 12.7V on BOTH ends (power passes all the way through it), the second is just Suzuki's spare clipped in an unwired holder (reads nothing — normal). So power is healthy from the battery through the fuse. (3) Followed the feed forward to the green 2-pin connector up by the bars (a red wire + an orange wire): the RED wire is the always-hot feed and reads 12.7V there — power is good right up to the steering head. (4) Wiggling the harness at the steering head makes the headlight flicker on and off = a make-and-break in a conductor right where the bundle flexes with steering. This matches the original 'died when I turned the bars' symptom, and the water that killed the speedo points to the same area. ORIGINAL SYMPTOM (first test ride, June 2026): leaned the bike, turned the bars, and ALL power died at once — headlight cut instantly, no response to ignition on/off. The speedo was already removed + taped off during that ride, so a speedo short was ruled out. The carbureted DR-Z400S has no tip-over/lean sensor, so the lean didn't cut it — the wiring moved. NEXT STEPS TO CLOSE IT: (a) Disconnect the battery negative before cutting anything. (b) Pinpoint the exact inch — steady the bundle, wiggle one wire at a time to find which single wire toggles the light, then binary-search it (pinch the midpoint, flex each half, follow the half that flickers; a gentle steady pull while flexing makes the break show up sharper). Breaks usually sit right where a wire enters the back of a connector, or at a hard bend / under an old taped section. (c) Cut out the bad section back to bright clean copper; splice with solder + adhesive-lined heat-shrink (seals against the moisture history) or an adhesive-lined heat-shrink butt connector; leave a little slack so it flexes over a length, not one point, and route clear of the steering-head turn-stops. (d) While it's open, clean the green connector pins (contact cleaner + dielectric grease) — same water exposure, cheap insurance. (e) TEST: continuity-check the repaired wire with the power off, then key on -> headlight solid, then turn the bars lock-to-lock to confirm it stays lit through the full sweep, then check horn + brake light (same feed). Once power is solid, the speedo rebuild moves back to the top. SAFETY while flexing it live: keep any bare wire from touching the frame/engine or it'll pop the main fuse and send you back to square one.

Summer 2025 — the extensive carb + cooling overhaul Paul recalled (his private EXTRACTED.md note had it only as a vague recollection); the OpenAI ChatGPT conversation mine reconstructed the blow-by-blow on 2026-07-22. THE ARC: the bike started hard and would run only on the choke — a classic LEAN condition (clogged pilot / stale gas). Paul cleaned the carburetor and spark plug and installed a NiceCNC extended air/fuel mixture screw, but the old screw had sat ~5.5 turns out and the new one was reset far leaner — it wouldn't catch and backfired. Chasing it richer to ~4 turns out over-corrected into FLOODING: raw fuel leaked from the carb, a flooded cylinder strained the starter (near-hydrolock), and the plug sprayed fuel. ⚠️ SAFETY: while cranking with the plug out to clear the flood, expelled fuel vapor IGNITED — a brief garage flash-fire near the plug (no injury; a hard lesson in not cranking raw fuel near an arcing/ungrounded plug). Separately, the RADIATOR was found visibly damaged on 2025-07-11 — new radiators installed BOTH sides by 2025-07-19, cooling system refilled and bled (an initial trapped air pocket caused smoking + a red temp light until re-bled; the radiator receipt is still unfound — see private service records for the narrowed 7/11–7/19 purchase window). Final loose end: a HIGH IDLE + overheat after the carb work, traced to the idle-speed screw turned in too far (NOT the fuel screw) — backed out to spec. OUTCOME: starts reliably, the start-squeak gone. Fuel-screw baseline for this bike at ~2,900 ft elevation ≈ 1.75–2.5 turns out. Installed + confirmed running: NiceCNC extended mixture screw, DRZ400 air filter, NGK CR8E plug, APE inline fuel filter.

RESOLVED SINCE (Paul-confirmed 2026-07-22): the vacuum petcock now works fine and the fuel-screw washer is back in — the bike is running very well. STILL OPEN: valve clearance has not been confirmed checked.

restoration.detail: Summer 2025 (captured from the ChatGPT mine 2026-07-22; identified as this G22A from an ID-tag photo 2025-09-12 — earlier threads mis-guessed 'G14/G16'). After a family oil change filled it to the dipstick MAX, the cart smoked heavily and sputtered at full throttle — an OVERFILL forced oil through the crankcase breather into the intake/combustion. Draining the carb didn't help (ruled out flooding); the fix was draining + flushing the oil, refilling a measured ~1 qt, and cleaning pooled oil out of the air intake — ran well after (Paul-confirmed). A residual oil-fouled main jet caused a lingering throttle sputter into July. Separately (2025-05-04): left in the rain, ran ~1 mi on low gas then died and wouldn't restart even with starter fluid — no logged resolution, likely subsumed by the June oil work. The 'fill by measure, not to MAX' lesson is now in maintenance.engineOil.
Added a few vent holes to the airbox to cure a post-filter-swap sputter — runs clean now. May open it up a little more to experiment with airflow; watch that it doesn't lean out or pull in dust.
